memories.memory_text: I swung the golf club hard into Slick’s jaw after he tried to shut Gordon up—felt the crack, saw him go still, and made sure everyone knew silence was not an option.
When Plank came back with the drugs and cash, I threw the steel across the room—heard it thunk into the wall, and let that silence say everything.

I stood there with the money and pills in front of me, telling Plank again that he’ll get more only when he finds a job worth doing—same as always, same as I’ve said before. He didn’t say a word, just stood there, so I knew he had no problem with it.
I asked Plank if he knew those geezers well, then pressed him on what they were into—turns out they're just soft poofs, public school types, nothing heavy.
I asked Plank about security and he said the gate’s never locked—fifty times he’s been there and it’s always open, those toffs too soft, believing in karma like it’ll protect them.
I remember stepping into view of the cupboard hole, seeing Bacon hunched over all that recording gear with his headphones clamped on, the lights flickering like the house was breathing.
I pointed at Paul and told them we’re using his van because it’s up some stairs, and we’ll stick out like balls on a bulldog—Plank goes first to unlock the cage, and he confirmed it’s never locked.
I set the heist for tomorrow at eight o’clock, told them the stags don’t get up till midday, and I like hitting them at their lowest ebb—then asked if everyone was savvy.
I helped load the van with the crew.
I snapped at Mick, telling him to stay still—he’s always jumping in without thinking, and I needed to know what was happening first.

I walked in, dropped my bags, and saw Plank bleeding and John rubbing his chest like something was wrong—right there in my front room.

I tore the tape off my head, fighting to get free, and then got the others loose—my hands were raw but I had to move fast.
I said they were dead already, didn't matter who they thought they were—I'd find them, I'd kill them every way I could think of, slow and brutal.
I told John to strip the house—tear it apart piece by piece—because a bug might’ve been left behind, and I don’t care if he thinks it’s pointless. I need control, and I need answers.
After the house is stripped, I told them to grab every thieving slag they could find and torture them—badly—because someone has to pay, and if they don’t find who’s responsible, it’ll be John.

I remember standing there, telling them this wasn't just a problem—it was the Mount fucking Everest of problems—because they had no idea who fucked us over, and that’s when I started slapping their heads, yelling at them to get out and find the bastards.

I was stunned when Big Chris appeared out of nowhere, grabbing both shotguns before I could react—he headbutted me hard, knocked me flat, and took the case of money.
I had the knife pressed along the kid's throat, lying low in the back seat, and when Big Chris laughed it off, I told him to get the money from the office or his son wouldn't see his next birthday.
Big Chris sped up and then slammed into a parked car—I got thrown forward hard, hitting the windscreen, the world jolting as the glass cracked against my face.

memories.memory_text: I told them I hadn't slept in two days, had broken ribs, and felt the flu coming on—still, the sergeant didn't care, just wanted answers like I had them. When he asked, all I could say was I was in a black hole, blindfolded.

I waved my money around like I was on fire, shouting 'Bargain, that's a bloody bargain'—ten pounds? I'll have five. I couldn't wait to grab them, felt like the whole crowd was watching me, and damn, it felt good.
One second I'm flying over stairs, the next I hear 'Bacon!'—then I see it in his eyes, same as mine: the cops. We didn't talk, just ran. I didn't even know they were there until that moment.

I looked in the bag Soap pulled from under him—cash, no count yet—and asked if he was really sure he could afford twenty-five grand, because money like that vanishes fast if it’s not backed by something solid.
I said a hundred grand, and that was it—no flinching, no explaining. The number hung there, and I knew they were weighing whether I was in or out.
I insisted on counting the money myself, even though Bacon said it wasn't necessary—I wasn't about to trust a pile on the table without knowing it was all there.
I said I was going to the john and just walked off—couldn't sit there anymore with all that silence pressing down on me.

I walked into JD's Bar and saw Tom, Soap, and Bacon staring at me like I'd grown a second head, then my dad stepped in asking if I was playing cards with Harry—like I was some kind of idiot who'd walk into that.

I was the only one they let through—cash in hand, smart clothes, and still the doorman waved the others off like they were nothing, told me to send them to that grim pub next door while I walked in alone.

I walked in, saw all those guys counting money, and couldn't help but notice the empty chair—and how everyone else was already seated, watching. When Hatchet called me JD's son, I knew it wasn't just recognition, it was a test.

I saw Tanya shuffling cards—blonde, there at the table—and tossed out a casual 'Evening Tanya, it's been a while.' No reaction, just focus on the deck. Hard to tell if she remembered me or just didn't care.
When my knees stop knocking I'll live with it. Four hundred blind.
I pushed two thousand blind, staring Don down without flinching, even though he was waiting for me to crack.
I must be about 250,000 up by now, but the game’s getting out of hand—IOUs are flying, and that’s when things turn ugly.
I looked at my cards and saw the run for the flush—Hatchet threw down twenty thousand, and I didn’t blink, just pushed mine in. Felt like the deck finally owed me one.
I pushed fifty grand into the pot, knowing Hatchet would smell blood if he saw me sweat, but my palms stayed dry even when he stared right at my forehead.
I said 'one hundred grand,' and thought I had him—then he dropped two hundred and fifty like it was nothing, staring right at my hairline like he could see the sweat before it even broke.
When the croupier said they'd have to see my cards unless someone loaned me the money, I felt the room tighten—no way out, just the cold choice between exposure and taking a loan from him.
I told the others Harry was going to start sizing up all our fingers because he knew I couldn't raise the money alone — the debt was on all of us now, not just me.
I was walking down the street with a bottle in my pocket, barely holding it together, and when I saw JD's door, I just... didn't go in.
I stood there with Tom, Bacon, and Soap watching me, and I told them I had a plan—no need to bring in the old man, just listen carefully.
I told them to hit the fuckers, and let the silence hang—knew it would sink in. They needed to feel the weight of it before someone broke.
Soap started panicking about guns, so I snapped back with that feather duster line—sarcasm to cut the tension, even if I knew he wasn't wrong.
I told them to tie 'em up and tape their faces, then I got the keys—everything went smooth, just like I wanted.
I told them the loot was going to my place because there was nowhere safer—it’s the last place they’d ever look, and I wasn’t about to let this fall apart now.
I saw Ed hand grass to Tom and I snapped it into an order—get it to Nick and burn it fast, no delays, no mistakes.
I pushed the pile of notes aside and said it was a good day's work—Harry was done, and I wanted to lock up and get drunk, not sit around smoking that awful stuff.
After we pay Hatchet, this deal puts us up near enough two hundred grand each. Not bad for a day's work, I think you will agree.
I saw the house—smoking, blood everywhere—and when Tom said the money and gear were gone, swapped for corpses, I didn’t hesitate. Bollocks, I’m not dying for this mess—I’m out.

I asked Ed what the hell was going on and if he'd told the old man yet—couldn't stand sitting there while he wasted time looking serious.
I asked how heavy the fellas were, because if we're going to do this, I need to know what kind of risk we're really walking into.
After Bacon said he was game, I said 'Me too'—once I heard the plan wasn't completely idiotic, I wasn't going to sit out.
I told Nick the stuff isn't normal weed—it's fucked-up skunk class A, so potent I can't even think straight, let alone move shit.
I asked Nick for a couple of sawn-off shotguns, and when he flipped out, I just looked at him and said, 'I think you're Nick the Greek.'
I remember holding those old Purdeys, thinking they looked fancy but wouldn't scare anyone who mattered — more likely to get me laughed at than feared.
I got those guns off Nick the Greek for seven hundred for the pair — they look nice, and that’s what matters. I don’t know if they work, but I like ‘em.
I told Eddy everything was fine out here, just 'right as rain'—even though I could hear the tension in his voice, asking where the hell they were supposed to hide.
I saw them arrive and said it plain—'They're here.' No need to dress it up, no time for chatter.
I swung the lead pipe hard into Paul's kneecaps the second he tried to bolt—guy went down screaming like a stuck pig, had to drag him in kicking and thrashing.

Ed shoved a bundle of grass into my hands and told me to get it to Nick fast—like I was some errand boy all of a sudden.
I just needed a moment to count the money without everyone yapping—there was a pile of notes shoved aside like it was nothing, and nobody was giving a shit about the actual take.

I asked about Rory Breaker, and Barfly Jack started spouting some cockney-rhyming slang bullshit about him torching some fat cunt who changed the channel during a football match—guy lit up like a gas main, and Rory just sat there, calm as a coma, watching the game.
I told them Rory Breaker wouldn’t screw us over—messing with us isn’t worth the headache, and nobody wants a pain in the arse, especially not some rich buyer.
I looked at that blood-covered house and knew it was fucked—no money, no weed, just corpses. I said 'What do we do now?' because we were screwed and someone had to say it.
I folded up the shotguns and put them on the rail, gave them one last wipe like it meant something—then pushed them over. Watched them fall.
I saw them catch on a ledge, just hanging there—so I climbed over the rail, one hand on the guns, one on the fucking railing, swaying like an idiot.
